title: Quiz — which of Verne's club details is real?
learning_goal: Know that Verne's Reform is half fantasy (porphyry columns, blue glass) and half exact (nine garden windows); know you can visit during Open House.

narration.script: Verne describes the club in loving detail: mosaic floors, a gallery under a dome held up by twenty red porphyry columns, blue painted windows, a dining room with nine windows onto a garden already gilded with autumn. Compare that with Barry's real building. Which of these details is real? Take your time; the tea is famous. Half fantasy, half exact — treat the novel that way for the next seventy-nine days. And one practical note: you can stand in that saloon yourself, one weekend a year, when the club opens for guided tours during Open House London; the caption has this year's dates. The tour, they say, includes one very long staircase.

interaction.prompt: Verne describes the Reform Club's interior. Which of these details is real?

options.text: Twenty red porphyry Ionic columns holding up a dome
options.feedback: Verne's invention. Barry's saloon has a two-storey peristyle — Ionic below, Corinthian above — in yellow marble and scagliola.

options.text: A gallery lit through blue painted windows
options.feedback: A garble. The saloon sits under a coved glass roof with an oval saucer-dome.

options.text: A dining-room with nine windows onto the garden
options.feedback: Exact. Nine tall casement windows in the coffee-room's south wall, and the garden is still there.
